subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Resources and Economics
subtitle: Natural resources, economic activity, trade, development, migration, and sustainable planning.
description: A source-faithful human geography pack about how natural resources shape settlement, jobs, trade, development, migration, and sustainability.

data.targetWord: an area of Earth that has one or more shared human or physical features

examples.en-GB: The Corn Belt is a farming region because many places there share agricultural features.

data.targetWord: the natural and human-made surroundings that shape how people live in a place

examples.en-GB: A coastal environment may include beaches, ocean water, roads, ports, and buildings.

data.targetWord: the usual pattern of weather in a place over a long period of time

examples.en-GB: Climate helps explain why some regions grow crops while others need irrigation.

data.targetWord: the number of people living in a particular area, settlement, region, or country

examples.en-GB: A city with several million residents has a large population.

data.targetWord: the number of people living within each unit of land area in a place

examples.en-GB: High population density means many people live close together in each square mile.

data.targetWord: something people use from the environment to meet needs, wants, or economic goals

examples.en-GB: Water, soil, timber, coal, wind, and sunlight can all become resources.

data.targetWord: a useful material or feature that comes from nature rather than being made by people

examples.en-GB: Oil, fish, copper, fertile soil, and timber are examples of natural resources.

data.targetWord: a resource that can be replaced naturally if people use and manage it carefully

examples.en-GB: Forests are renewable only when trees are replanted and protected as they regrow.

data.targetWord: a resource that forms so slowly it cannot be replaced within a human lifetime

examples.en-GB: Coal, oil, natural gas, and many metal ores are nonrenewable resources.

data.targetWord: work people do to produce, sell, move, exchange, or provide goods and services

examples.en-GB: Farming, mining, teaching, manufacturing, banking, and transportation are economic activities.

data.targetWord: the part of the economy that collects raw materials directly from nature

examples.en-GB: Farming, fishing, forestry, and mining are primary sector activities.

data.targetWord: the part of the economy that turns raw materials into manufactured products or buildings

examples.en-GB: Food processing and car production belong to the secondary sector.

data.targetWord: the part of the economy that provides services rather than extracting or manufacturing goods

examples.en-GB: Health care, education, retail, and transportation are tertiary sector services.

data.targetWord: the part of the economy based on knowledge, research, information, data, and technology

examples.en-GB: Software design, scientific research, and data analysis are quaternary sector jobs.

data.targetWord: the buying, selling, and exchanging of goods and services between people or places

examples.en-GB: Trade allows countries to sell resources they have and buy resources they lack.

data.targetWord: a good or service sold from one place to another region or country

examples.en-GB: Wheat grown in Kansas may be exported to other countries.

data.targetWord: a good or service bought from another place, region, or country

examples.en-GB: A country may import oil, coffee, electronics, or food it cannot produce easily.

data.targetWord: the steps that move a product from raw materials to production, sale, use, and disposal

examples.en-GB: A cotton T-shirt supply chain includes farming, spinning, sewing, shipping, and retail.

data.targetWord: the basic systems and networks that help a place function and support economic activity

examples.en-GB: Roads, bridges, ports, power lines, internet, and water systems are infrastructure.

data.targetWord: the movement of people from one place to another for temporary or permanent settlement

examples.en-GB: Workers may migrate to cities when jobs and services act as pull factors.

data.targetWord: using resources to meet present needs while protecting future people and ecosystems

examples.en-GB: Replanting trees after logging is one way to support sustainability.

data.targetWord: improvement in quality of life, economic wellbeing, services, infrastructure, and opportunity

examples.en-GB: Better health care, education, income, and infrastructure can show development.

data.targetWord: the total value of goods and services produced within a country during a period

examples.en-GB: GDP can show economic output, but not whether wealth is shared fairly.

data.targetWord: how comfortable, secure, and healthy daily life is for people in a place

examples.en-GB: Housing, safety, income, health care, and services affect standard of living.

data.targetWord: the ways people affect environments and environments influence people, choices, and economies

examples.en-GB: Building dams creates electricity but can also change river ecosystems.

data.targetWord: a situation where there is not enough of a resource to meet wants or needs

examples.en-GB: Freshwater scarcity can affect farms, cities, industries, and ecosystems.

data.targetWord: protecting resources and using them carefully so they remain available in the future

examples.en-GB: Fixing leaks during drought is a practical example of water conservation.

data.targetWord: the study and physical structure of rocks that helps explain where minerals and fuels form

examples.en-GB: Geology affects where coal seams, oil reserves, and metal ores are found.

data.targetWord: a natural feature of Earths surface such as a mountain, plain, valley, river, or coast

examples.en-GB: Landforms affect farming, mining, settlement, and transportation routes.

data.targetWord: the amount of usable water that people, farms, industries, and ecosystems can access

examples.en-GB: Low water availability can limit farming and make city growth harder.

data.targetWord: soil with nutrients and structure that support healthy plant growth and food production

examples.en-GB: Fertile soil makes grain farming easier in parts of the Great Plains.

data.targetWord: a relationship where places rely on each other for resources, goods, services, or markets

examples.en-GB: A city may depend on rural farms for food and export services in return.

data.targetWord: a pattern where valuable resources do not lead to broad prosperity because of dependence or conflict

examples.en-GB: The resource curse can happen when oil profits benefit only a small group.

data.targetWord: to develop different industries or income sources instead of depending on only one activity

examples.en-GB: Oil-exporting countries may diversify into tourism, finance, renewable energy, or technology.

data.targetWord: the artificial supply of water to crops when rainfall is not enough for farming

examples.en-GB: Centre-pivot irrigation creates circular fields in some dry farming regions.

data.targetWord: a long period with less rainfall than usual that can reduce water supplies and crop yields

examples.en-GB: Drought can lower reservoir levels and push farmers to use more groundwater.

data.targetWord: water stored underground in soil or rock that people may pump for farms and cities

examples.en-GB: Groundwater can decline if it is pumped faster than it naturally refills.

data.targetWord: an underground layer of rock or sediment that stores and transmits usable groundwater

examples.en-GB: A farming region may depend on an aquifer for irrigation water.

data.targetWord: the farming practice of changing crops between seasons to protect soil and manage nutrients

examples.en-GB: Crop rotation can reduce soil exhaustion and support sustainable farming.

data.targetWord: a farming method that plants crops with minimal soil disturbance to reduce erosion

examples.en-GB: No-till farming helps keep soil in place during wind and rain.

data.targetWord: a row of trees or barriers planted to slow wind and protect soil or crops

examples.en-GB: Windbreaks can reduce soil erosion on open farmland.

data.targetWord: the wearing away of topsoil by wind, water, or poor land management

examples.en-GB: Soil erosion can reduce crop yields and damage long-term farm productivity.

data.targetWord: catching fish faster than populations can reproduce and replace themselves naturally

examples.en-GB: Overfishing can shrink fish stocks and harm coastal fishing economies.

data.targetWord: the variety of living things in an ecosystem, region, or on Earth as a whole

examples.en-GB: The Amazon Basin is important because of forests, freshwater, and biodiversity.

data.targetWord: a nonrenewable energy resource formed from ancient living matter over millions of years

examples.en-GB: Coal, oil, and natural gas are fossil fuels used for energy and industry.

data.targetWord: a shift from one main energy system toward another, often from fossil fuels to renewables

examples.en-GB: An energy transition may create renewable jobs while fossil fuel workers need retraining.

data.targetWord: reliable access to enough affordable energy for homes, businesses, transportation, and public services

examples.en-GB: Local renewable energy can improve energy security by reducing dependence on imports.

data.targetWord: minerals used in many technologies that can be difficult and costly to mine and process safely

examples.en-GB: Rare earth minerals are used in smartphones, wind turbines, and electric vehicles.

data.targetWord: the stage where raw materials are cleaned, refined, changed, or prepared for manufacturing

examples.en-GB: Cotton must be cleaned and spun before it can become fabric.

data.targetWord: making goods from raw materials or parts, usually in factories or workshops

examples.en-GB: Manufacturing turns metals, plastics, cotton, and components into finished products.

data.targetWord: a path or network used to move people, goods, resources, and information between places

examples.en-GB: Rivers, railroads, highways, ports, and shipping lanes can become transportation routes.

data.targetWord: a coastal or river facility where ships load, unload, and transfer goods or passengers

examples.en-GB: Ports help connect resources and products to global markets.

data.targetWord: a person or group affected by a decision or able to influence its outcome

examples.en-GB: Farmers, workers, Indigenous communities, scientists, and local families can be stakeholders.

data.targetWord: a rule or law used to guide activities and reduce risks to people or environments

examples.en-GB: Mining regulations can require safe waste storage and water quality monitoring.

data.targetWord: repairing damaged land, water, habitats, or communities after resource use or development

examples.en-GB: Land restoration after mining can reduce long-term environmental damage.

data.targetWord: a change in resource or energy systems that supports workers, families, and communities

examples.en-GB: A fair transition may retrain fossil fuel workers for renewable energy jobs.

data.targetWord: the level at which a geographic decision or pattern is studied, from local to global

examples.en-GB: Water sharing can be studied at local, regional, national, and global scales.

data.title: From Resource to Product
data.instruction: Put the supply chain stages in the correct order.
items: Raw material is collected from nature or grown on a farm.
The material is processed, cleaned, refined, or prepared.
Manufacturing turns the material into a usable product.
Transportation moves the product through ports, roads, trains, or warehouses.
Retail or service businesses make the product available to customers.
The consumer uses the product and later reuses, recycles, or throws it away.

data.title: Resource Use Feedback Loop
data.instruction: Order the stages in a resource-based growth cycle.
items: A resource is discovered or becomes valuable.
Investment supports extraction, production, or access.
Jobs and income increase in the area.
Population may grow as workers and families move in.
Demand rises for housing, water, energy, and services.
Environmental pressure increases and the community chooses conservation, regulation, restoration, or rapid use.

data.title: Economic Change in a Region
data.instruction: Put these common stages of economic change in order.
items: Early settlement grows near rivers, fertile land, forests, minerals, or other resources.
Roads, railways, ports, or factories develop during a growth period.
Industrial expansion increases factory work and energy use.
Service growth adds more schools, hospitals, stores, finance, and tourism jobs.
A knowledge economy develops through education, internet access, universities, research, and data jobs.
A sustainable transition focuses on cleaner energy, conservation, and long-term planning.

data.title: Town Mining Decision
data.instruction: Order the steps a town should take before approving a new mine.
items: Identify stakeholders such as workers, families, Indigenous communities, farmers, scientists, government, and businesses.
Collect evidence about jobs, tax income, water use, traffic, waste rock, habitats, and cleanup costs.
Hold public discussions so benefits, risks, and trade-offs are heard.
Compare approval, rejection, and modified project options.
If approved, set rules for monitoring, water protection, restoration, worker safety, and cleanup funding.
